topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; frameworks and competencies may have limited direct application to Australian organisational settings, though core digital competency principles could be transferable.
takeaways: European public health organisations identify specific technical and data literacy competencies as foundational; consider mapping which of these are most critical for your Australian workforce's AI adoption priorities.

Scoping reviews of this type typically reveal gaps between required and existing competencies in health sectors; assess whether similar gaps exist in your organisation and identify targeted upskilling opportunities.

Competency frameworks developed in European public health may emphasise regulatory compliance (e.g., GDPR) that differs from Australian privacy law; adapt any framework recommendations to local governance requirements.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to dental education context. Findings may not directly transfer to other professional disciplines or non-clinical AI literacy programmes, though the competency framework methodology could have broader applicability.
takeaways: Consider adopting a structured competency framework approach when designing AI literacy programmes — breaking AI capabilities into specific, teachable competencies helps employees understand which skills they need to develop.

Embed AI literacy into domain-specific contexts (in this case, dental practice) rather than teaching generic AI concepts in isolation — this makes the material more relevant and memorable for learners.
Use competency frameworks to identify skill gaps across your workforce and prioritise which AI capabilities matter most for your organisation's operations.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect client-based case studies rather than systematic research. Applicability depends on organisational context and sector.
takeaways: Treat AI adoption as a people challenge first: success requires upskilling existing staff and redesigning roles, not just implementing technology.
Identify which employee groups need which AI capabilities: different roles require different literacy levels, from basic AI awareness to advanced technical skills.
Create clear pathways for workforce transition: plan how current employees will adapt to AI-enabled roles rather than assuming displacement or autonomous adoption.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development unclear without seeing full methodology and geographic scope.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-specialists works best when embedded within broader digital literacy frameworks rather than taught in isolation, suggesting workplace AI training should integrate with existing digital competency programs.

Holistic competency frameworks should balance technical understanding with critical thinking and ethical reasoning — consider how your organisation's AI literacy program addresses all three dimensions, not just technical skills.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education contexts; findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-academic settings without additional evidence.
takeaways: Design faculty development programs that address underlying concerns and resistance to AI adoption, moving beyond content delivery to build genuine readiness and confidence in teaching AI concepts.
Position faculty as the critical lever for embedding AI literacy into curricula — their own capability gaps and mindset shifts are prerequisites for effective student learning.
Create structured pathways to help educators transition from viewing AI as a threat to viewing it as a tool they can competently teach and integrate into public health practice.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on higher education context; applicability to corporate AI capability development in non-academic settings would require adaptation.
takeaways: Consider a four-domain framework for AI literacy (technical, ethical, strategic, and operational) when designing capability programs; this meta-skill approach may help employees understand how AI competencies interconnect across their organisation.
Target AI literacy as foundational rather than specialist training — frame it as essential for managers and academics to innovate and lead, not just for technical roles.

Use this model to audit gaps in your current AI upskilling approach; identify which domains your employees need most development in (e.g. ethical reasoning vs. technical tools) to prioritise intervention.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The rise of AI in the workplace: why perceived organizational support fails to protect long-term career satisfaction - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The rise of AI in the workplace: why perceived organizational support fails to protect long-term career satisfaction  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet provided. Further information on sample size, geographic location, industry sectors, and study design would be needed to determine the breadth of applicability.
takeaways: Perceived organisational support alone may not sustain career satisfaction during AI adoption—consider complementary interventions such as concrete upskilling programs, transparent communication about role changes, and career pathway clarity to maintain long-term employee engagement.

Monitor the gap between espoused support (what the organisation says) and experienced support (what employees actually receive during AI implementation) through regular feedback mechanisms, as this disconnect may be a key driver of declining satisfaction.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are limited to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other healthcare or non-healthcare professions. The three-wave design strengthens causal inference within nursing, but sector-specific factors (clinical workflows, patient safety concerns) may limit applicability to other AI adoption contexts.
takeaways: Support work autonomy when introducing AI tools — nurses' sense of control over how AI is implemented predicts better wellbeing outcomes, suggesting that top-down AI adoption without staff input may undermine psychological safety and engagement.

Frame AI readiness training around preserving professional judgment rather than replacing it — positioning AI as a tool that augments rather than constrains clinical decision-making correlates with improved wellbeing during adoption.
Measure and monitor wellbeing at multiple time points during AI rollout to identify whether autonomy is being eroded, rather than assuming readiness training alone will sustain positive outcomes.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — no information provided about sample size, geography, sectors studied, or research design. Full paper review needed to assess applicability to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Address role ambiguity explicitly when introducing generative AI tools — unclear expectations about AI responsibilities and human roles can undermine adoption and collaboration effectiveness.

Invest in building employee self-efficacy with AI systems through training and practical experience, as confidence in using these tools appears to be a key driver of productive employee-AI collaboration.
Monitor both role clarity and confidence levels during AI implementation; the 'dual pathways' framework suggests these are distinct mechanisms requiring separate management strategies.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: General conceptual discussion — no empirical data provided. Observations likely apply broadly to organisations using AI tools, but specific risks depend on company context, industry, and AI deployment approach.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational policies distinguishing appropriate uses of workplace AI tools (task assistance) from inappropriate ones (mental health support, personal counselling), and communicate these boundaries explicitly to staff.

Provide employees with information about AI limitations (hallucinations, bias, lack of confidentiality) so they make informed decisions about when to use AI for personal matters versus seeking human support or professional help.

Create accessible pathways to human support (EAP, managers, HR, mental health services) and actively promote them as the preferred channel for personal or emotional concerns, signalling organisational care and reducing reliance on impersonal AI tools for vulnerable situations.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — depends on sample characteristics, sector, and geographic scope not provided in the title or excerpt.
takeaways: The Automation–Augmentation Paradox suggests that AI tools can both replace employee knowledge work and enhance it; understanding which effect dominates in your organisation helps you design training and role design to favour augmentation over deskilling.

Monitor whether generative AI adoption is eroding critical thinking or domain expertise among employees — this requires intentional intervention (e.g., structured reflection, quality assurance roles) to ensure AI augments rather than automates away valuable knowledge practices.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not clear from title/snippet. The moderating variables (self-efficacy, transformational leadership) are universal psychological constructs applicable across contexts, but findings may vary by industry, organisational culture, and AI implementation approach.
takeaways: Build employee self-efficacy around AI tools through targeted training and skill-building programs — this can buffer against job insecurity even when AI is being introduced.

Leaders adopting transformational leadership behaviours (vision-setting, individualised support, intellectual stimulation) can meaningfully reduce job insecurity during AI implementation — consider leadership development focused on these competencies during technology transitions.
Job insecurity from AI adoption is not inevitable; organisations can proactively manage it through human development and leadership practices, not just technology deployment.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner guidance based on consulting experience, but specific case studies, sample sizes, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Shift focus from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (building new human behaviours and mindsets) — this reframing helps employees move beyond compliance to genuine capability development.
Design change programmes that explicitly target behavioural shifts required for AI use, rather than treating behaviour change as a secondary outcome of technology rollout.
Identify which specific human behaviours and ways of working need to change in your context, then build targeted interventions around those — not just around learning the technology itself.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey insights draw on client work across sectors and geographies, but specific case examples and client contexts may not reflect all organisational types or Australian regulatory environments.
takeaways: Use a phased horizon framework (adoption → scaling → embedding impact) to structure your AI transformation roadmap rather than treating it as a single change event — this helps teams understand what success looks like at each stage and adjust support accordingly.

Identify which horizon your organisation is in now and tailor behaviour change interventions to that phase — early adoption requires different messaging and incentives than driving sustained behavioural change at scale.

Map concrete business outcomes to each horizon to help employees see how their behaviour change (e.g. learning new skills, adjusting workflows) connects to organisational impact — vague transformation goals typically fail to motivate sustained effort.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The theoretical framework (JD-R theory and cognitive appraisal) is widely applicable, but findings may be limited by geographic scope, industry type, and organisational context of the sample.
takeaways: Employee awareness of AI impacts job crafting through two distinct pathways: cognitive appraisal of stress and job demands-resources dynamics — understanding which pathway dominates in your organisation can help tailor change communication and support.

Stress appraisal matters: how employees cognitively interpret AI-related threats or challenges influences whether they proactively reshape their roles; framing AI adoption as a challenge to master (rather than a threat) may encourage constructive job crafting behaviours.

Job demands-resources theory suggests you should pair AI introduction with tangible resources (training, autonomy, peer support) to shift employee appraisal from threat to opportunity and support adaptive job crafting.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - gsb.stanford.edu
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  gsb.stanford.edu
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Findings and recommendations may reflect US academic and business contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific work tasks in your organisation that AI could augment rather than replace, then design targeted upskilling programs to help employees transition into higher-value roles.

Create structured opportunities for employees to experiment with AI tools in low-risk environments, as exposure and early wins can shift mindsets from threat to opportunity in behaviour change efforts.

Establish clear communication about how AI adoption will affect different roles, roles, and career paths — ambiguity is a major barrier to behaviour change and engagement during digital transformation.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings could be limited by specific organisational contexts, industry type, or geographic region of the sample.
takeaways: Recognise that AI adoption can trigger both approach (seeking new opportunities) and avoidance (withdrawing from tasks) responses in employees — tailor change communication to emphasise skill development and role expansion rather than job displacement risk.

Design job crafting opportunities proactively during AI rollout: allow employees to reshape their roles toward higher-value activities and skill-building rather than leaving them anxious about automation, which drives avoidance behaviours.

Monitor for avoidance patterns (task disengagement, resistance) as an early warning sign of psychological threat perception — intervene with transparent skill-mapping and retraining pathways to shift mindset toward approach-oriented job crafting.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's client engagements and case studies across multiple sectors, but findings reflect primarily large organisations with resources for AI adoption; may not generalise to SMEs or less digitally mature firms.
takeaways: Design workforce transformation as a parallel process to AI adoption: reskilling and role redesign must occur simultaneously with technology deployment, not after, to prevent adoption resistance and capability gaps.

Establish cross-functional change teams early that include frontline employees, not just executives and technical staff, to identify practical implementation barriers and build buy-in from those most affected by AI tools.

Create explicit pathways for role evolution rather than job elimination messaging; communicate how AI will augment existing roles and which new capabilities employees need to develop within the next 12–24 months.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a news summary of a single study; original research details, sample characteristics, and geographic scope are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism — typically seen as off-putting — may actually attract romantic partners in the short term, suggesting we're drawn to confidence and dominance even when they signal relationship red flags.

The finding challenges the intuition that toxic personality traits are universally unattractive, hinting at a mismatch between what we consciously value in partners and what our snap judgments reward.
This is a good reminder that initial attraction and long-term compatibility are completely different animals — what catches attention isn't what makes relationships thrive.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full text — would depend on sample size, participant demographics, and experimental methodology used to measure personality and memory for unexpected events.
takeaways: Some people genuinely remember surprising moments better than others, and your personality type predicts which camp you'll fall into — counterintuitively, it's not just about how shocked you were in the moment.
This challenges the common assumption that 'surprise' alone locks memories in place equally for everyone — your trait characteristics shape what unexpected events stick with you and why.
Your personality profile acts as a filter on what your brain flags as memorable, suggesting our minds don't record surprising events like video cameras, but selectively depending on who we are.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Unclear — snippet provides insufficient detail about sample size, geographic scope, or methodology to assess generalisability of neuroimaging findings.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies can reveal structural or functional differences associated with psychopathy, challenging the assumption that personality traits are purely behavioural.

The term 'shocking difference' suggests a counterintuitive finding — perhaps brain differences are smaller or larger than expected, or located in unexpected regions, making this potentially surprising even to neuroscience researchers.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology and sample details not provided. Wine review analysis may reflect linguistic patterns in English-language reviews rather than universal personality traits.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from seemingly mundane text like wine reviews — the everyday language people use to describe sensory experiences reveals something about who they are.

Wine tasting vocabulary is more psychologically revealing than you'd expect — how people describe taste and flavour preference contains subtle personality signals, making this a fun example of hidden data in everyday writing.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — twin study methodology provides insights into genetic vs. environmental contributions to authoritarianism, but generalisability depends on sample composition and country of origin, which are not specified.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that political authoritarianism has both genetic and environmental roots — it's not purely a matter of upbringing or ideology, which challenges the common assumption that beliefs are entirely learned.

The 'surprising' angle suggests researchers found genetics plays a more significant role than expected, or that environmental factors operate differently than assumed — a counterintuitive result that reframes how we think about where political attitudes come from.

articles.title: Personality traits shape how pilots react to simulated in-flight crises - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Personality traits shape how pilots react to simulated in-flight crises  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings depend on the specific simulator setup, pilot sample characteristics, and crisis scenarios tested. Results may not generalise to real in-flight emergencies where stakes and stress are vastly higher.
takeaways: Personality isn't destiny in a crisis — pilots with the 'wrong' traits can still perform well if trained properly, suggesting that selection and training matter as much as natural temperament.

The finding that personality predicts crisis response in a controlled setting is intuitive, but the real surprise would be *which* personality traits help most (e.g., does neuroticism hurt or does conscientiousness save the day?), making this a useful checkpoint for aviation psychology.

This research reminds us that high-pressure decision-making isn't purely about knowledge — who you are as a person shapes how you think under extreme stress, which has ripple effects across safety-critical industries beyond aviation.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not evident from the title and snippet alone. The focus on leader power distance orientation suggests potential cross-cultural relevance, but without knowing the sample size, geographic scope, and sectors studied, the breadth of application cannot be fully assessed.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership drives innovation through psychological safety — prioritise creating environments where team members feel safe speaking up, admitting mistakes, and challenging ideas without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.

Leader power distance orientation matters: leaders who minimise hierarchical barriers and position themselves as approachable and equal to their teams are more likely to foster the psychological safety needed for innovative thinking.

Assess your own leadership approach — if you maintain high power distance (formal hierarchy, limited accessibility), you may inadvertently suppress the team openness required for innovation, even if your intentions are inclusive.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad global scope typical of PwC surveys, but generalisability may be limited by self-selection bias in survey respondents and potential overrepresentation of white-collar/professional workers. Geographic and sectoral breakdowns unknown from snippet.
takeaways: Identify which workforce anxieties (job security, AI impact, career progression) dominate your employee population by comparing PwC's global findings to your own organisation's pulse survey or focus group data.

Use the survey's findings on employee hopes and fears as a baseline for designing targeted psychological safety interventions—e.g. if AI anxiety is prevalent, structure learning and upskilling programs that position employees as collaborators rather than replacements.

Benchmark your organisation's psychological safety culture against PwC's global themes to identify gaps; for instance, if the survey highlights trust deficits around leadership transparency, prioritise open communication about AI adoption and role changes.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The proposed mechanism (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) may vary significantly by organisational culture, sector, and implementation approach. Findings likely most relevant to knowledge-work settings.
takeaways: When implementing AI, actively communicate the rationale and involve employees early — unmanaged AI adoption creates uncertainty that erodes psychological safety and can increase mental health risks.

Ethical leadership practices during AI rollout (transparency about capabilities, job security, decision-making processes) are protective factors; organisations should embed ethics governance before, not after, deployment.
Monitor psychological safety metrics before and after AI initiatives; watch for early signs of disengagement or anxiety, particularly among staff whose roles are directly affected by automation.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience and proprietary data, but geographic scope and sample composition are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Use psychological safety initiatives to reduce barriers that prevent underrepresented or disadvantaged employees from participating fully — this 'levelling the playing field' effect can be a concrete business case when pitching safety work to leadership.

Consider how psychological safety might interact with equity and inclusion efforts; framing safety as a fairness mechanism (not just engagement) may resonate differently with stakeholders and HR partners.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte reports draw on consulting experience but lack detailed methodology disclosure; findings likely reflect practices among large organisations that engage Deloitte, limiting applicability to smaller or public-sector teams.
takeaways: Prioritise human skill development (communication, collaboration, adaptability) as a foundation for psychological safety before or alongside technical capability building.

High-performing teams require intentional capability development across the team — not just individual upskilling — suggesting peer learning and collective trust-building should be embedded in team development programmes.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely moderate — general frameworks for AI-driven workplaces, but specific organisational contexts, sector differences, and implementation barriers not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Implement structured co-skilling programmes that pair technical AI training with role-specific upskilling to reduce perceived job threat and build workforce confidence.
Proactively communicate organisational AI adoption strategy and redeployment pathways to employees — absence of clarity amplifies job insecurity and erodes psychological safety.
Combine skill development with visible organisational support (e.g. mentoring, career progression planning) to signal that workers remain valued during AI transitions, not disposable.
